title: The Last Ferry
text:
The ferry horn sounded twice, and Mara knew she had ten minutes before the boat pulled away from Halden Island for the last time that season.

Her grandfather was not on the dock. She scanned the gravel lot, the shuttered bait shop, the line of trucks rolling up the ramp, and found nothing but gulls arguing over a dropped sandwich. Every October he made the same crossing to spend the winter with her family on the mainland, and every October he cut it close. But this year was different. This year, Mom had said on the phone, he wasn't sure he was coming at all.

"He's lived forty years on that rock," Mom had said. "You don't just pack forty years into a suitcase."

Mara had rolled her eyes then. Now, standing in the wind with her hands jammed into her pockets, she wasn't so sure it was funny.

The horn sounded again. A deckhand waved at her impatiently.

Then she saw him—not walking from the road, as she had expected, but climbing up from the rocky beach below the lighthouse, moving slowly with a canvas bag over one shoulder. He stopped at the top of the path and turned to look back at the water, the lighthouse, the gray cottages scattered along the hill like dropped dice. He stood there so long that Mara started toward him.

"Grandpa! The boat—"

"I know about the boat," he said, without turning. "Boats leave. That's what they do." He reached into the bag and pulled out a smooth white stone, round as an egg. "Found this my first summer here. I put it back on the beach every fall, and every spring it's waiting for me in nearly the same spot."

"You didn't put it back this time," Mara said.

He looked at the stone for a long moment, then pressed it into her palm. Her fingers closed over it, still warm from his hand.

"No," he said. "This time I thought someone else should hold on to it."

They walked to the ferry together, and he did not look back again.

title: What the Orchard Keeps
text:
My father planted the orchard
the spring before I was born—
fifty saplings, thin as pencils,
in a field that had only known corn.

"A tree is a promise," he told me,
"you make to someone you'll never meet."
I laughed at him once, at fifteen,
for waiting ten years for something to eat.

Now I walk the rows in October.
The branches bow low to the ground.
The bark has grown rough as his knuckles;
the trunks lean the way he leaned
when he stood in the field, listening for rain.

I fill my basket slowly.
Some promises take a lifetime to keep.
Some are kept by the ones who receive them.

title: Why Cities Run Hot
text:
On a summer afternoon, the center of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the farmland just a few miles away. Scientists call this effect an urban heat island, and it is becoming one of the most important challenges facing growing cities.

The main cause is the material cities are made of. Asphalt roads, concrete sidewalks, and dark rooftops absorb large amounts of sunlight during the day and release that stored heat slowly, long after sunset. In contrast, fields and forests are covered in plants that release water vapor through their leaves, a process that cools the surrounding air much as sweat cools skin. When vegetation is replaced by pavement, that natural cooling disappears.

Human activity adds to the problem. Air conditioners, cars, and factories all release waste heat into the streets. Tall buildings can also block wind, trapping warm air between them. As a result, the difference between city and countryside temperatures is often greatest at night, when rural areas cool quickly but cities stay warm.

These extra degrees are not just uncomfortable. Hotter cities use more electricity for cooling, which can strain power grids during heat waves. Higher temperatures also speed up the chemical reactions that form ground-level ozone, a pollutant that irritates the lungs. Most seriously, extreme heat is dangerous to human health, especially for older adults and people without access to air conditioning.

Fortunately, cities are experimenting with solutions. Some are painting rooftops white or light gray so that they reflect sunlight instead of absorbing it. Others are planting street trees, which provide shade and restore some of the cooling effect of vegetation. A few cities have even built "green roofs" covered with soil and plants. None of these strategies can erase the heat island entirely, but together they can make city summers noticeably cooler—and safer.

title: Who Owns the Time?
text:
Before the 1880s, there was no such thing as standard time in the United States. Each town set its clocks by the sun, declaring noon to be the moment the sun stood highest in the sky. Because the sun appears to move across the sky from east to west, noon in Boston arrived several minutes before noon in New York, which arrived before noon in Philadelphia. For most of history, this "local time" caused few problems. A farmer had little reason to care what time it was fifty miles away.

The railroads changed that. A single train might pass through dozens of towns, each keeping its own time, so railroad companies began publishing schedules based on their own "railroad times." By the early 1880s, travelers faced dozens of different railroad times across the country. A passenger changing trains could find that the station clock, the train clock, and the clock in the town square all disagreed. Missed connections were common, and on lines where trains shared a single track, confusion about the time could even contribute to accidents.

In 1883, the railroads decided to solve the problem themselves. On November 18—a date some later called "the day of two noons"—railroads across the United States and Canada reset their clocks to a new system of standard time zones. In many cities, crowds gathered to watch as clocks were stopped and then restarted to match the new time.

Not everyone welcomed the change. Some newspapers complained that the railroads, which were private businesses, had no right to change the time for an entire nation. Critics insisted that time belonged to the sun, not to a corporation. Nevertheless, the convenience of standard time was hard to resist, and most towns soon adopted it. Remarkably, the U.S. government did not make time zones official law until 1918—thirty-five years after the railroads had already made them part of daily life.
